purpose: Role-based institutional topology closing the explanatory gaps between central banks, sovereign debt, bond holders, development finance, payment/settlement plumbing, prudential standards, legal-entity identity and large non-bank capital pools.
design_rule: Add an institution only when it closes a distinct causal or evidentiary gap. Messaging is not settlement; settlement is not custody; custody is not beneficial ownership; a development-bank bond is not the same obligation as its downstream project loan; a standard setter is not a supervisor; an asset manager is not the legal owner of every asset it manages.

layers.label: Holder-side capital and external position data
layers.gap_closed: BIS IDS identifies issuers but not bond holders. We need a holder-side dataset to answer which economy owns securities issued by another economy.
layers.map_role: Directed portfolio-holding edges only where counterpart economy and instrument class are published.

nodes.name: IMF Portfolio Investment Positions by Counterpart Economy (PIP; formerly CPIS)
nodes.role: Cross-border holdings of equities, investment fund shares and short/long-term debt securities by counterpart issuer economy.
nodes.why: This is the cleanest official bridge from issuer-side bond data to country-level holder-side portfolio positions.
nodes.caveat: Portfolio positions are reported by participating economies and remain subject to coverage, valuation and confidentiality limitations. A country position does not identify the underlying private legal entity.

nodes.name: IMF International Investment Position framework
nodes.role: Country external financial assets and liabilities by functional category.
nodes.why: Provides the balance-sheet frame around portfolio holdings, direct investment, reserves and other investment so isolated bond holdings can be interpreted as part of a country's external position.
nodes.caveat: Aggregate external position is not automatically bilateral unless the underlying source exposes counterpart geography.

layers.label: Official liquidity and multilateral development finance
layers.gap_closed: The project has sovereign issuers and central banks but lacks the institutions that lend to governments, issue supranational bonds, transform shareholder capital into project finance, and provide crisis liquidity.
layers.graph_pattern: shareholders/capital -> multilateral institution -> bond investors/funding -> loan/guarantee/grant -> sovereign/project borrower

nodes.name: International Monetary Fund
nodes.why: Explains official crisis lending, reserve support, IMF quotas and SDR positions that otherwise appear as unexplained sovereign obligations or reserve assets.

nodes.name: International Bank for Reconstruction and Development
nodes.why: IBRD raises funds in capital markets and lends onward to sovereign/sub-sovereign borrowers, creating a two-leg obligation chain the graph must preserve.

nodes.name: International Development Association
nodes.why: Separates concessional development obligations from market-rate sovereign debt and from IBRD lending.

nodes.name: European Investment Bank
nodes.why: A major financing bridge between EU member-state capital, capital markets and infrastructure/industrial projects; already mentioned in the North Europe atlas but not yet modeled as an obligation transformer.

nodes.name: Nordic Investment Bank
nodes.why: This is the most direct existing financial institution connecting the Nordic-Baltic North geography. It belongs close to the North obligation graph, not as a symbolic Axis claim but as a real member-owned lender.

nodes.name: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development
nodes.why: Connects European/North shareholders with investment in Central/Eastern Europe and wider regions, making it important for Ukraine/reconstruction and cross-axis capital flows.

layers.label: Messaging, payment, FX and securities infrastructure
layers.gap_closed: A debt or security can exist without explaining how instructions, cash and securities actually move. These institutions form the rails between counterparties.

nodes.name: Swift
nodes.role: Secure standardized messaging between financial institutions and market infrastructures.
nodes.why: Explains communication paths but must not be shown as moving or holding the underlying money merely because a payment message traverses Swift.
nodes.caveat: Messaging is not settlement and Swift is not itself the debtor, creditor or beneficial owner.

nodes.name: CLSSettlement
nodes.role: Payment-versus-payment settlement for 18 major currencies through central-bank accounts.
nodes.why: Closes the FX settlement-risk gap and links DKK, EUR, USD, CAD, GBP, NOK, SEK, CHF, JPY and other major currencies through a real settlement mechanism.

nodes.name: Euroclear
nodes.role: Issuance, settlement, custody, asset servicing and collateral infrastructure for securities.
nodes.why: Provides the post-trade layer between a bond issuer and the chain of intermediaries/holders; essential for understanding why custody location is not beneficial ownership.

nodes.name: Clearstream
nodes.role: CSD/ICSD settlement, custody, collateral, repo and securities-lending infrastructure.
nodes.why: Together with Euroclear, closes the Eurobond/post-trade custody gap for European and international securities.

nodes.name: Fedwire Funds Service
nodes.role: Final same-day USD transfers across Federal Reserve accounts.
nodes.why: Completes the dollar payment rail beneath Treasury, bank and interbank obligations; unlike Swift, Fedwire effects settlement in central-bank money.

nodes.name: DTCC clearing and settlement infrastructure
nodes.role: Central counterparty, netting, clearing and settlement infrastructure in major U.S. securities markets.
nodes.why: Explains how U.S. securities obligations are netted and settled after trade execution and why gross trading volume is not the same as final cash obligation.

layers.label: Standards, supervision and resolution
layers.gap_closed: The graph currently shows institutions and exposures but not the rules that constrain bank capital, market infrastructure, supervision or failure resolution.

nodes.name: Financial Stability Board
nodes.role: Coordinates national authorities and international standard setters on global financial stability.
nodes.why: Provides the coordination layer above sector-specific standards; it should be modeled as policy/coordination, not as a regulator with direct universal legal authority.

nodes.name: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision
nodes.role: Global prudential banking standards and supervisory cooperation.
nodes.why: Bank capital, liquidity and exposure data cannot be interpreted well without the Basel framework that shapes internationally active banks.

nodes.name: Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures
nodes.role: Standards and policy for payment, clearing and settlement infrastructure.
nodes.why: Provides the rule layer governing the safety/efficiency of the same payment and settlement systems the map will display.

nodes.name: European Banking Authority
nodes.role: EU banking Single Rulebook, risk assessment and supervisory convergence.
nodes.why: Separates EU-level rulemaking/convergence from national supervision and ECB Banking Supervision.

nodes.name: European Securities and Markets Authority
nodes.role: EU securities-market regulation, supervision and convergence.
nodes.why: Needed once bonds, funds, trading venues, rating agencies and securities infrastructures become first-class graph objects.

nodes.name: European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority
nodes.why: Pension funds and insurers are major bond holders; their regulatory layer is necessary when holder-sector data becomes visible.

nodes.name: Single Resolution Board
nodes.role: Central resolution authority in the Banking Union.
nodes.why: Adds the failure/restructuring path: a stressed bank can move from exposure to resolution without treating taxpayer support or creditor bail-in as automatic.

layers.label: Legal identity and ownership resolution
layers.gap_closed: Names are not stable enough for a global obligation graph; banks, funds and issuers need persistent legal-entity identity and parent relationships.

nodes.name: Global Legal Entity Identifier Foundation / Global LEI System
nodes.role: Global identifiers and reference/ownership relationship data for legal entities.
nodes.why: This is the canonical answer to entity resolution. It reduces duplicate nodes and supports 'who is who' and 'who owns whom' without guessing from names.

layers.label: Large non-bank capital pools
layers.gap_closed: Country-level creditor data still hides the actual institutional investors holding bonds and equities. Large pension and sovereign funds are important named holder nodes where public holdings data exist.

nodes.name: Government Pension Fund Global / Norges Bank Investment Management
nodes.role: Large global owner of equities and fixed-income securities on behalf of Norway.
nodes.why: A major North-origin capital pool with highly transparent holdings; it can turn country-level portfolio exposure into a named institutional-holder graph where the data support it.

nodes.name: ATP Livslang Pension
nodes.role: Large Danish pension institution investing across bonds, swaps, equities, real estate and infrastructure.
nodes.why: Provides a concrete Danish holder-side institutional node and connects pensions, long-duration liabilities, bonds and infrastructure investment.

layers.label: Global development-bank expansion
layers.gap_closed: Once the architecture works for EIB/NIB/EBRD/World Bank, equivalent regional lenders are required for a genuinely global map.

nodes.name: Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank
nodes.why: Infrastructure lender and capital-markets bridge across Asia and beyond.

nodes.name: Asian Development Bank
nodes.why: Major Asia-Pacific sovereign/private development-finance node.

nodes.name: African Development Bank
nodes.why: Major African sovereign/private development-finance node that also issues in international capital markets.

nodes.name: Inter-American Development Bank
nodes.why: Major public-sector development lender in Latin America and the Caribbean.

missing_functions_after_this_wave.why: Needed for complete bank-failure waterfalls, but it becomes useful only after named banking-system and deposit-liability data exist.
LCH, CME and other CCPs matter for derivatives/collateral networks, but adding them before derivative exposure data would create decorative nodes.
Required for auction calendars and sovereign maturity walls; add them country-by-country where debt issuance becomes detailed.
Ratings affect funding costs and eligibility but should enter as observations/assessments rather than becoming causal substitutes for market pricing.

map_placement.rule: Institutional importance does not justify permanent map clutter. Nodes surface when selected, traced, filtered or required by an active relationship.
